newsitem.title: USA: Atlantis heads for Mir, despite problem.
newsitem.headline: Atlantis heads for Mir, despite problem.

text.p: Shuttle Atlantis on Tuesday closed in on the orbiting Russian space station, where U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid eagerly awaited her ride home.
The shuttle remained on target to dock with Mir late on Wednesday despite the mysterious and unexpected shutdown of a crucial component in the reusable spaceship's hydraulic system.
Atlantis is to pick up Lucid, now in her fifth month aboard the station, and drop off her replacement, veteran astronaut John Blaha, for a four-month stay.
The shuttle was 16,000 miles (25,750 km) from Mir when the astronauts awoke Monday evening and was closing in on the station by 571 miles (918.9 km) with every 90-minute revolution of the globe.

The crew of six spent their first full day in space checking out experiments and supplies in a pressurized compartment housed in the shuttle's cargo bay. The so-called Spacehab module was doubled in size for this mission to accommodate more supplies for Mir.
Tuesday's flight plan also included a test of the docking system needed for the link-up and the filling of containers with drinking water for the Mir crew.
Engineers at mission control in Houston were trying to determine what caused one of the shuttle's three auxiliary power units to cutout shortly after Atlantis reached orbit Monday.

NASA's flight rules require the mission to be curtailed if one of the devices fails, but a recent addition to the rule book would allow the mission to go ahead as planned if shuttle managers "agree that it is a safe and reasonable course of action."

The auxiliary power units are part of the shuttle's hydraulic system, which moves its engines, wing flaps and rudder during launch and landing. The devices are not needed in orbit and the shuttle can land safely with just two operational units. A second failure, however, could place the shuttle in danger.

Space agency officials were to meet in Houston on Tuesday morning to discuss what impact, if any, the loss of one power unit will have on the planned 10-day mission. The return of Lucid, however, was not in doubt, space agency officials said, but an early end to the mission was still possible.

The shuttle and Mir were supposed to be docked five days while Lucid and Blaha switched places and thousands of pounds (kgs) of equipment and supplies were transferred to and from the station. A shortened mission would force the astronauts to rush that work.
"I think with heroic efforts we could get almost everything transferred in a day," flight director Paul Dye said before the launch. "But that would not be a very pleasant way to do business."

Atlantis thundered into space before dawn on Monday, ending nearly seven weeks of delays caused by shuttle booster problems, a menacing offshore hurricane and difficulty finding a launch date on the busy schedule at Cape Canaveral.
Lucid caught a glimpse of the shuttle's fiery ascent as Mir sailed through space high above the Kennedy Space Centre. She spent Tuesday getting ready for the shuttle's arrival.
"She's doing some last-minute packing," said NASA spokeswoman Kari Fluegel at Russia's mission control, just outside of Moscow.
Atlantis, making its fourth visit to Mir, is due to dock with the orbiting outpost at around 11:17 p.m. EDT Wednesday (0317 GMT Thursday).
Lucid, a 53-year-old mother of three, was originally due home in early August. She is the first of six U.S. astronaut who will staff the Russian space outpost into 1998.
The shuttle's late arrival gave Lucid an extra entry in the record books for the longest space mission by a woman. She had already broken the record for the longest stay in space by an American.
If all goes according to plan, Atlantis will return home with Lucid on September 26.
